statement_record.book: Two categories are constructed. (a) Par: objects are sets; an arrow f : A → B is a partial function, i.e. a function |f| : U_f → B on a subset U_f ⊆ A; 1_A is the total identity; the composite g∘f has domain |f|^{-1}(U_g), obtained as the pullback of U_g ↪ B along |f|, and composition is associative with the identities as units. (b) Sets_*: objects are pointed sets (A,a), arrows are functions f : A → B with f(a) = b.
statement_record.intree: [Part] : Category with obj := Sets, hom x y := SetoidMorphism x (option y), id := Some, compose := Kleisli bind — 'This is the category PAR (also written Par or Pfn) of setoids and partial maps ... a partial map A ⇀ B is encoded as a total setoid map A → option B'; and [Par] : Category with obj := Type, hom A B := A → option B, id := Some, compose := option_bind f ∘ g. For (b) only the generic [Coslice C c] : Category exists.

statement_record.book: For a set I viewed as a discrete category, Sets^I is the category of I-indexed families of sets and I-indexed families of functions, and it is equivalent (not isomorphic) to the slice Sets/I, via Φ((A_i)) = (∐_i A_i → I) and Ψ(α : A → I) = (α^{-1}{i})_i. More generally the slice E/E makes 'E-indexed family of objects of E' precise in any category E, where the functor-category presentation is unavailable; and if E has pullbacks, reindexing along f : E → F is the pullback functor f^* : E/F ⟶ E/E.
statement_record.intree: Slice C c is defined as the category of objects-over-c; Star_Functor f : Slice C a ⟶ Slice C c is the base-change/pullback functor f^*, with its action on morphisms produced by the pullback UMP (ump_pullbacks) under the standing Hypothesis that the relevant pullbacks exist; DiscreteCat A and the functor category [C, D] both exist, so [DiscreteCat I, Sets] is expressible.

evidence.intree_statement: Class EquivalenceOfCategories {C D : Category} (F : C ⟶ D) := { quasi_inverse : D ⟶ C; equivalence_counit : F ◯ quasi_inverse ≈ Id[D]; equivalence_unit : Id[C] ≈ quasi_inverse ◯ F }.  (bundled as Theory/Equivalence/Bundled.v:36 Definition CategoryEquivalence (C D : Category) : Type := ∃ F : C ⟶ D, EquivalenceOfCategories F, with Notation "C ≃ D")

Definition Equivalence_to_Cat_Iso {C D : Category} {F : C ⟶ D} (E : EquivalenceOfCategories F) : C ≅[Cat] D := @Build_Isomorphism Cat C D F (@quasi_inverse C D F E) (@equivalence_counit C D F E) (symmetry (@equivalence_unit C D F E)).  (converse at :172 Cat_Iso_to_Equivalence; round trips at :182, :187)
Lemma op_invol {C : Category} : (C^op)^op = C.  (over Definition Opposite `(C : Category) : Category at :106, with Notation "C ^op")

statement_record.book: A large class of examples of equivalences comes from classical duality theorems; these are typically NOT isomorphisms C ≅ D^op (still less equalities C = D^op) but equivalences C ≃ D^op, because the construction establishing the duality recovers the original object only up to isomorphism. The finite boolean-algebra result to follow is a special case of Stone Duality.
statement_record.intree: The vocabulary the example needs is all present and asserted: C ≃ D as ∃F, EquivalenceOfCategories F; C^op with (C^op)^op = C on the nose; and the equivalence/isomorphism gradation realized concretely as Cat versus StrictCat — Equivalence_to_Cat_Iso/Cat_Iso_to_Equivalence assert that an equivalence IS precisely an isomorphism in Cat (whose hom-setoid Functor_Setoid identifies functors up to natural isomorphism), while Instance/StrictCat.v:57 Instance StrictCat := { obj := Category; hom := @Functor; homset := @Functor_StrictEq_Setoid; ... } is the strict 1-category 'in which an isomorphism is a genuine (on-the-nose) isomorphism of categories'.
statement_record.strength_comparison: intree-weaker: every ingredient of the example's assertion is formalized, but the assertion itself — that duality theorems take the shape C ≃ D^op and are not on-the-nose isomorphisms — is nowhere instantiated. Note a presentational subtlety the reader must not miss: because Cat's hom-setoid is up-to-natural-isomorphism, the library's `≅[Cat]` already MEANS equivalence, so the distinction the example draws lives between StrictCat and Cat, not between `≅` and `≃`; a naive reading of an in-tree `C ≅[Cat] D` as 'isomorphism of categories' in Awodey's sense would be wrong.

gap: No duality theorem of the shape C ≃ D^op (or C ≅[Cat] D^op) is proven anywhere in-tree: there is no concrete pair of categories exhibited as equivalent to an opposite. The two candidates are prose only — the self-duality of relations is stated in Instance/Rel.v:38's header ('self-duality `Rel ≅ Rel^op`') with no corresponding functor or isomorphism among that file's definitions (Rel:45, Rel_Initial:90, Rel_Cartesian:97, Rel_Cocartesian:127, Rel_Closed:146, Relation_Functor:167), and Stone duality appears only in Theory/Equivalence.v:119-122's background essay. So the example's motivational claim about the SHAPE of duality results is expressible in-tree but unwitnessed.

statement_record.book: For the forgetful functors U : Groups ⟶ Monoids and V : Monoids ⟶ Sets, decide for each of the six properties — faithful, full, injective on arrows, surjective on arrows, injective on objects, surjective on objects — whether it holds.
statement_record.intree: Mon : Category (internal monoids in a monoidal C) with Mon_Forget : Mon ⟶ C and Mon_Forget_Faithful : Faithful Mon_Forget, proved because morphism equivalence in Mon IS equivalence of the underlying C-morphisms. GroupObject exists as a class with a coercion to MonoidObject, but no category of groups and no functor between them.
statement_record.strength_comparison: intree-weaker: exactly one of the twelve determinations the exercise requires is settled (V is faithful), and it is settled in greater generality than the book asks (any monoidal C, not just Sets). Nothing at all is settled about U, because there is no category of groups and no forgetful functor Groups ⟶ Monoids; and four of the six properties have no in-tree vocabulary whatsoever.

gap: Only one of the exercise's twelve determinations exists in-tree. (a) There is no category of groups: Structure/Group.v gives the class GroupObject (with a coercion GroupObject >-> MonoidObject, which is U on objects) but no Grp category and no functor U : Grp ⟶ Mon, so none of U's six properties — in particular the interesting answer, that U is FULL because a monoid homomorphism between groups automatically preserves inverses — is stated or proved. (b) For V, only faithfulness is proved; the mathematically interesting negative answers (V is not full, not surjective on arrows, not surjective on objects) are absent, and the library never proves any functor NOT full. (c) Four of the six properties are not expressible: Theory/Functor.v defines only Full (:331, as a chosen section prefmap of fmap) and Faithful (:342, as injectivity of fmap); there is no predicate for a functor being injective on arrows, surjective on arrows, injective on objects, or surjective on objects, and the only in-tree object-level condition is EssentiallySurjective (Theory/Equivalence.v:141), which is strictly weaker than surjective-on-objects. (d) Instance/CMon.v:169 CMon_Forget : CMon ⟶ Sets is a genuine Monoids-to-Sets forgetful functor for commutative monoids, but its faithfulness is asserted only in the surrounding comment, never proved.
